title: Payment card number served in a response
description: The response body carries a full payment card number in Visa, Mastercard or Discover grouping. A card number in a page or API payload is enough to attempt a card-not-present charge, and it cannot be revoked like a password.
remediation: Store only the last four digits and a payment-processor token; never render the primary account number back to a browser or API client.
limitation: One response body. The rule does not attempt a Luhn check or a live authorisation, so an invalid but well-shaped number is still reported.
scopeT: A response body that contains a four-group card number together with a payment-related word.
fp: Documentation that shows a masked number such as **** **** **** 4242 is not reported, because four masked groups carry only the last four digits.
recordDesc: A PAN in a response links a cardholder to the site and survives in browser caches, proxies and logs. Even a test card in production markup tells an attacker which processor and format the site accepts.
applicability: Checkout receipts, order-history pages and payment API responses.
risk: The caller obtains a usable card number for the account holder, and any proxy or cache between the server and the browser keeps a second copy.
why: A browser or API client never needs a full PAN to render a receipt.
fix: Return only the last four digits and the card brand.
Keep the PAN inside the payment processor and out of application logs.
verifyT: Request the receipt and confirm the body carries no more than four digits of the card number.

observation.body:
Accepted cards

We accept Visa and Mastercard. Your saved card shows **** **** **** 4242.

title: International bank account number served in a response
description: The response body carries an IBAN next to a bank marker. An IBAN is a complete, checksummed transfer target: it names the country, the bank and the account, and no further detail is needed to move money.
remediation: Show the last four characters of the account and the bank name only, and require re-authentication before payout details are revealed.
limitation: One response body. The rule checks the country prefix and the grouping; it does not run the ISO 13616 modulus check.
scopeT: A response body with a two-letter country code, two check digits and grouped account characters, plus a bank marker.
fp: A page that shows the IBAN structure with a placeholder is not reported, because at least three groups of account characters must follow the check digits.
recordDesc: The IBAN is the routing instruction itself. With it a third party can set up a direct debit or redirect a payout, and the check digits make transcription errors unlikely.
applicability: Payout dashboards, invoice screens and vendor master data.
risk: The caller obtains a verified transfer target for the account holder.
why: Screens can name the bank without printing a transfer-ready identifier.
fix: Mask the IBAN to the last four characters.
Gate payout-detail changes behind a second factor.
verifyT: Open the payout screen and confirm the IBAN is masked.

observation.body:
IBAN format

An IBAN begins with two country letters and two check digits, then the bank and account groups.

title: US Social Security number served in a response
description: The response body carries a Social Security number in the canonical three-two-four grouping next to a marker that names it. The SSN is the identifier US financial and employment systems trust most.
remediation: Mask all but the last four digits in every response and keep the full number in an encrypted store with access logging.
limitation: One response body. The rule needs the SSN marker so that an unrelated nine-digit grouping is not reported.
scopeT: A response body containing an SSN-shaped number and a Social Security marker.
fp: A page describing the SSN format without an instance is not reported, because a full three-two-four number must be present.
recordDesc: An SSN in a response enables identity takeover: it is accepted as proof of identity by many institutions and cannot be reissued.
applicability: HR portals, tax forms, loan applications and support tooling that echoes customer records.
risk: The caller obtains the identifier needed to open credit, file taxes or impersonate the person.
why: No application screen needs the full SSN after enrolment.
fix: Store the SSN encrypted and return only the last four digits.
Log every read of the full value.
verifyT: Request the profile page and confirm only the last four digits are rendered.

observation.body:

title: Aadhaar number served in a response
description: The response body carries a twelve-digit Aadhaar number next to its marker. Aadhaar is the Indian identity number used for KYC, subsidies and SIM registration.
remediation: Return a masked Aadhaar (last four digits), and store the full number only in a consent-tracked vault.
limitation: One response body. The rule does not run the Verhoeff checksum, so a well-shaped but invalid number is still reported.
scopeT: A response body containing a twelve-digit Aadhaar-shaped number and an Aadhaar marker.
fp: A page explaining the twelve-digit format without an instance is not reported, because the digit sequence must be present.
recordDesc: Aadhaar numbers are used as an authentication factor in many Indian services; exposing one enables SIM swaps and benefit fraud.
applicability: KYC status pages, beneficiary lists and onboarding APIs.
risk: The caller obtains an identity number that other services treat as proof of identity.
why: KYC screens only need to show the enrolled state and the last four digits.
fix: Mask the number in every response.
Restrict full Aadhaar reads to a consent-logged service.
verifyT: Open the KYC page and confirm only the last four digits are shown.

observation.body:
Aadhaar

title: Bangladesh National ID number served in a response
description: The response body carries a Bangladesh National ID number (10, 13 or 17 digits) next to its marker. The NID is the primary identity document for bank accounts, SIM registration and government services in Bangladesh.
remediation: Return only the last four digits and keep the full NID in an encrypted column with read auditing.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the documented digit lengths next to an NID marker; it does not check the issuing authority.
scopeT: A response body containing a National ID digit sequence and an NID marker.
fp: A page describing how many digits the NID has is not reported, because no digit sequence follows the marker.
recordDesc: A leaked NID lets a third party pass identity checks at banks and mobile operators, and it is printed on documents that are hard to replace.
applicability: Bank onboarding, SIM registration and citizen-service portals.
risk: The caller obtains a full identity number that other services accept as proof of identity.
why: Applications verify the NID once and afterwards need only a masked reference.
fix: Mask the NID in every rendered record.
Keep full values behind a consent-checked service.
verifyT: Request the profile and confirm the NID is masked.

National ID

title: Bangladesh mobile number served in a response
description: The response body carries a Bangladesh mobile number in national or international form next to a phone marker. Mobile numbers are the recovery channel for most accounts in the region.
remediation: Mask the middle digits, or omit the number entirely when the screen only confirms that a number is on file.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the 880/0 + 1[3-9] numbering plan and does not validate the operator prefix against the current allocation.
scopeT: A response body containing a Bangladesh mobile number and a phone marker.
fp: A page that explains the numbering plan with placeholder zeros is not reported, because the operator digit must be 3 to 9.
recordDesc: A mobile number is enough to target an SMS one-time code and to correlate the account with other services that use the same number.
applicability: Profile pages, order confirmations and support tools.
risk: The caller learns the recovery number and can attempt SIM-swap or OTP-interception attacks.
why: The screen can confirm the number without printing it in full.
fix: Show the number as 01XXX-XXXXXX with the middle masked.
Require a fresh challenge before displaying or changing it.
verifyT: Open the profile and confirm the number is partially masked.

observation.body:
Mobile numbers

Bangladeshi mobile numbers start with 01 followed by the operator digit. Example: 01XXXXXXXXX.

title: Bulk email address list served in a response
description: The response body carries seven or more email addresses in one comma-separated run. A list of addresses is a ready-made target set for phishing and credential stuffing.
remediation: Paginate or permission-gate contact lists, and render recipients one at a time instead of dumping the whole set.
limitation: One response body. The rule counts addresses in a single run; a page with several isolated addresses is not reported.
scopeT: A response body with a run of at least seven comma-separated email addresses.
fp: A page with a single contact address is not reported, because the rule requires a repeated run.
recordDesc: A harvested address list converts directly into a phishing campaign, and each address also confirms that the person has an account here.
applicability: Newsletter previews, admin member lists and notification recipient dumps.
risk: The caller walks away with a verified customer list for social engineering.
why: Recipient sets belong behind authorisation, not in a page body.
fix: Return recipient counts instead of addresses.
Authorise and audit any bulk export.
verifyT: Request the member list and confirm addresses are paginated or omitted.

title: Passport machine-readable zone served in a response
description: The response body carries a passport machine-readable zone line. The MRZ encodes the document number, name, nationality, date of birth, sex and expiry date, and is accepted as a key by many verification services.
remediation: Return only the extracted, verified fields the screen needs, and never echo the raw MRZ.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the two-character document code and the filler characters that identify an MRZ line.
scopeT: A response body containing a P< document line with MRZ filler characters.
fp: A page describing the MRZ layout with a placeholder such as P<XXX is not reported, because at least six filler or name characters must follow.
recordDesc: The MRZ is a compact identity document: it repeats the data printed on the photo page and is machine-verifiable without the passport itself.
applicability: Visa portals, hotel check-in and travel-booking confirmations.
risk: The caller can reproduce the document data for identity verification and travel bookings.
why: Screens need the parsed fields, not the machine zone.
fix: Parse the MRZ server-side and discard the raw line.
Return only the fields the screen displays.
verifyT: Upload a passport and confirm the response carries no P< line.

observation.body:
Machine-readable zone

The first line begins with the document code, for example P<XXX, followed by the issuing state.

Audit reads of the full value.

scopeT: A response body containing a three-three-three digit group and a SIN marker.

applicability: Payroll, tax slips and bank onboarding.

Log full-value reads.

Social Insurance Number

title: Medical record number served in a response
description: The response body carries a medical record number together with its marker. The MRN is the join key between appointments, lab results and billing in a hospital system.
remediation: Return an opaque per-session reference instead of the MRN, or mask it to the last three characters.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the printed MRN label; it does not verify the number against a hospital index.
scopeT: A response body containing an MRN label and a six-or-more character identifier.

risk: The caller can correlate health records and impersonate the patient at a reception desk.

title: Bank account and IFSC pair served in a response
description: The response body carries an Indian IFSC branch code together with an account marker. The pair is what a transfer instruction needs, and it is often enough to set up a payee.
remediation: Show only the last four digits of the account and never print the IFSC beside a full account number.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the eleven-character IFSC layout and an account marker in the same body.
scopeT: A response body with an IFSC code and an account marker.
fp: A page that lists branch IFSC codes without an account number is not reported, because the account marker must also be present.
recordDesc: Routing code plus account number is a complete transfer target, and it also reveals which bank branch holds the account.
applicability: Payout dashboards, vendor master screens and refund APIs.
risk: The caller can redirect or imitate payouts, and learns the account holder branch.
why: Screens need a masked account and a bank name, not a transfer-ready pair.
fix: Mask the account number to four digits.
Require re-authentication before revealing payout details.
verifyT: Open the payout screen and confirm the account is masked.

Branch codes

title: Vehicle identification number served in a response
description: The response body carries a seventeen-character VIN next to its marker. The VIN maps to the registration, service history and often the owner record.
remediation: Mask the last six characters when the screen only needs to identify the model.
limitation: One response body. The rule relies on the VIN marker so that other seventeen-character identifiers are not reported.
scopeT: A response body with a VIN marker and a seventeen-character identifier.
fp: A page explaining what a VIN is, without a value after the marker, is not reported.
recordDesc: A VIN gives access to service history and ownership lookups in many countries, and it is printed on the vehicle in public view.
applicability: Service booking, insurance quotes and fleet dashboards.
risk: The caller can enumerate vehicle history or impersonate the owner at a service desk.

fix: Show the last six characters.
Require an owner check before full VIN disclosure.

title: Device IMEI served in a response
description: The response body carries a fifteen-digit IMEI next to its marker. The IMEI identifies a physical handset and follows the device across SIM changes and owners.
remediation: Show the last four digits only, and keep the full IMEI in a device-registry service.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the printed IMEI label with fifteen digits and does not run the Luhn check.
scopeT: A response body with an IMEI label and fifteen digits.
fp: A page describing where to find the IMEI is not reported, because no fifteen-digit value follows the label.
recordDesc: An IMEI links a device to its owner history and is used to block or track handsets.
applicability: Device registration, warranty and repair portals.
risk: The caller can impersonate the device owner or block the handset.
why: Repair screens can identify the device without the full hardware identity.
fix: Mask the IMEI to four digits.
Restrict full IMEI reads to support roles.
verifyT: Open the device page and confirm the IMEI is masked.

Find your IMEI

title: Date of birth column served in a CSV response
description: The response body is a CSV export whose header carries a date-of-birth column with populated dates. Date of birth is a common knowledge-based verification factor and a direct identifier.
remediation: Remove the column from bulk exports, and mask the value in screens that do not need it.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the header and the first dated row; it does not count rows.
scopeT: A response body containing a dob or date_of_birth header cell with a dated value.
fp: A page that mentions a date-of-birth field in prose is not reported, because the header and the delimiter must match.
recordDesc: A bulk export with birth dates hands over the most-used knowledge factor and enables targeted identity fraud across services.
applicability: Analytics exports, admin CSV downloads and marketing extracts.
risk: The caller obtains a verified list of names and birth dates for account takeover attempts.
why: Marketing and analytics rarely need the exact date, only an age band.
fix: Export an age band instead of the date.
Gate and audit bulk exports.
verifyT: Download the export and confirm no birth-date column is present.

observation.body:
Exports

title: User export with a password column served in a response
description: The response body is a CSV export whose header pairs an email column with a password column. The file is a ready-to-use credential list for the site.
remediation: Never include credential columns in exports; if a hash must leave the system, re-hash into a one-way store with a documented purpose.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the header row and does not attempt to crack the values.
scopeT: A response body containing an email,password header pair.
fp: A help page that quotes the header pair in prose without a delimiter is not reported, because the comma must be present.
recordDesc: An exported credential column turns a database read into account takeover, and it spreads the exposure to every reuse of the same password.
applicability: Admin exports, migration dumps and support tooling.
risk: The caller receives a file that can be replayed against the login form at scale.
why: No export needs a password column.
fix: Reject export definitions that include credential columns.
Alert on any query that selects a password column.
verifyT: Attempt the export and confirm the password column is refused.

scopeT: A response body with a salary or payroll field and a four-digit-or-longer amount.

applicability: HR dashboards, payroll APIs and analytics cubes.
risk: The caller learns individual compensation and can target employees with tailored fraud.

Audit reads by role.
verifyT: Request the employee payload and confirm no salary field is returned.

Analyst

title: Access token field served in a JSON response
description: The response JSON carries an access_token field. Access tokens are bearer credentials: anyone who reads the response can act as the user until the token expires.
remediation: Return tokens only in the token endpoint over a confidential client channel, and keep them out of pages and logs.

title: Refresh token field served in a JSON response
description: The response JSON carries a refresh_token field. A refresh token outlives the access token and can mint new sessions until it is revoked.
remediation: Keep refresh tokens in an httpOnly, same-site cookie bound to the client, and never in a JSON body that page scripts can read.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the field name and a long value; it does not exchange the token.
scopeT: A JSON body with a refresh_token key and a value of twenty characters or more.
fp: A description of the rotation flow without a token value is not reported.
recordDesc: A refresh token converts a short exposure into a long-lived session that survives password changes.
applicability: Session bootstrap endpoints and debugging consoles.
risk: The caller can keep minting access tokens after the original session ends.
why: Long-lived credentials must not be readable by page script.
fix: Deliver refresh tokens in an httpOnly cookie.
Rotate on every use and revoke on logout.
verifyT: Inspect the session bootstrap response and confirm no refresh token is present.

observation.body:
Sessions

The refresh token is set as an httpOnly cookie and is not returned in JSON.

title: TOTP seed served in a JSON response
description: The response JSON carries a TOTP seed. With the seed anyone can generate valid one-time codes, so the second factor collapses into the first.
remediation: Return the seed once, only to the enrolling session, and store it encrypted; never re-send it on later reads.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the field name and a base32-shaped value; it does not verify a code.
scopeT: A JSON body with a totp secret field and a base32 value of sixteen characters or more.
fp: A page that explains where to find the setup key is not reported.
recordDesc: A TOTP seed defeats the purpose of the second factor and survives every password change.
applicability: MFA management screens and admin user tooling.
risk: The caller can pass the second factor for the account indefinitely.
why: Seeds are write-only after enrolment.
fix: Encrypt seeds at rest and return them only at enrolment.
Require re-authentication to re-enrol.
verifyT: Open the MFA page of an enrolled user and confirm no seed is returned.

observation.body:
Authenticator app

Scan the QR code shown during enrolment. The setup key is displayed once.

title: Session identifier served in a JSON response
description: The response JSON carries a session identifier. Session ids are bearer credentials; a JSON copy is readable by page script and by anything that logs the response.
remediation: Keep session identifiers in httpOnly cookies and return only a session label to the client.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the field name and a long value; it does not replay the session.
scopeT: A JSON body with a session id field and a twenty-character-or-longer value.
fp: A page that discusses session identifiers in prose is not reported.
recordDesc: A session id in a body bypasses the httpOnly protection that keeps cookies away from script.
applicability: Debug headers, API session listings and support tools.
risk: The caller can hijack the session from a log or a cross-site script.
why: Session material should never be rendered as data.
fix: Store the session id in an httpOnly cookie only.
Expose a short local label for support.
verifyT: Request the session endpoint and confirm the id is absent.

observation.body:
Sessions

The session_id is stored in an httpOnly cookie and is never part of a JSON response.

title: JSON Web Token served in a response body
description: The body carries a three-part JSON Web Token. The header and payload are readable by anyone who sees the token; only the signature keeps the claims trustworthy.
remediation: Keep tokens server-side and return the claims the screen needs, not the token itself.
limitation: One response body. The rule recognises the three base64url segments and does not verify the signature.
scopeT: A body containing three dot-separated base64url segments that start with a JWT header.
fp: A page that shows only the header segment as an example is not reported, because all three segments must be present.
recordDesc: A bearer token in a body is a session for anyone who reads it, and its claims may include personal data.
applicability: Debug pages, API proxies and single-page bootstrap payloads.
risk: The caller can replay the token and read the claims inside it.
why: The browser can hold a token without the page printing it.
fix: Proxy calls server-side.
Return decoded, non-sensitive claims instead of the token.
verifyT: Request the page and confirm no three-segment token is present.

observation.body:
Tokens

A JWT has three parts separated by dots: header, payload and signature.

title: bcrypt password hash served in a response
description: The response carries a bcrypt hash with its cost parameter. The cost and salt are public by design, but the hash is the credential record and is crackable offline once it leaves the database.
remediation: Never serialise credential columns; if a hash must be shown for support, show only the algorithm and cost.
limitation: One response body. The rule recognises the modular crypt format and does not attempt cracking.
scopeT: A body containing a $2a$, $2b$ or $2y$ prefixed bcrypt string.
fp: A page that discusses bcrypt parameters without a hash is not reported.
recordDesc: Hashes are portable: once exported they can be attacked at leisure on a GPU without touching the site again.
applicability: Admin user lists, export endpoints and debug dumps.
risk: The caller can crack weak passwords offline and reuse them elsewhere.
why: Password hashes never belong in a response.
fix: Exclude credential columns from every serialiser.
Alert on queries that select password hashes.
verifyT: Request the user list and confirm no bcrypt string is present.

observation.body:
Password storage

We use bcrypt with a cost of 12. Hashes never leave the database.

title: Argon2 password hash served in a response
description: The response carries an Argon2 modular hash including memory, iteration and parallelism parameters. As with any password hash, it is an offline attack target once exported.
remediation: Exclude credential columns from responses and keep the parameters server-side.
limitation: One response body. The rule recognises the $argon2 family prefix and does not attempt cracking.
scopeT: A body containing an $argon2id, $argon2i or $argon2d modular hash.
fp: A page that explains Argon2 parameters without a hash is not reported.
recordDesc: A hash export shifts the attack from the rate-limited login form to an unthrottled offline run.
applicability: User APIs, migration tooling and support dumps.
risk: The caller can attack the credential record offline.
why: Hashes are secrets even though they are not reversible.
fix: Whitelist response fields.
Keep hashes in a column that no endpoint selects.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and confirm no modular hash is present.

observation.body:
Argon2

We use argon2id with m=65536, t=3 and p=4. Parameters are pinned in code.

title: MD5 password digest served with its password marker
description: The response pairs a password marker with a bare 32-character hexadecimal digest. MD5 is fast and unsalted values fall to precomputed tables almost immediately.
remediation: Migrate to a memory-hard hash and never expose the digest; re-hash on next successful login.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the marker and the digest; it does not look the digest up.
scopeT: A body containing a password marker and a 32-hexadecimal-character value.
fp: A page that discusses MD5 in prose without a digest is not reported.
recordDesc: A fast unsalted digest is effectively a password in a thin disguise for anything but a long random secret.
applicability: Legacy user tables, exports and debug views.
risk: The caller recovers common passwords from a table in seconds.
why: Fast hashes stopped being acceptable for passwords years ago.
fix: Re-hash with Argon2 or bcrypt on next login.
Remove digests from every response.
verifyT: Request the record and confirm no 32-hex digest follows a password marker.

observation.body:
Password policy

Passwords are stored with a slow hash. Older MD5 records are upgraded at login.

title: SHA-1 password digest served with its password marker
description: The response pairs a password marker with a bare 40-character hexadecimal digest. Like MD5, SHA-1 is far too fast to protect a password and is cheap to attack in bulk.
remediation: Re-hash on next login with Argon2id and remove the digest from every response.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the marker and the digest; it does not verify the value.
scopeT: A body containing a password marker and a 40-hexadecimal-character value.
fp: A page that mentions SHA-1 without a digest value is not reported.
recordDesc: A fast digest lets an attacker test billions of candidates per second away from the login form.
applicability: Legacy identity tables and migration exports.
risk: The caller can recover weak passwords offline.
why: General-purpose digests are not password hashes.
fix: Migrate the column to Argon2id.
Never serialise credential columns.
verifyT: Confirm no 40-hex digest follows a password marker in any response.

observation.body:
Digests

SHA-1 produces a 40-character hexadecimal digest and is not used for passwords here.

title: Basic authentication credential served in a response body
description: The body carries an Authorization header with a Basic value. Basic credentials are base64-encoded, not encrypted, so the user name and password are recoverable by anyone who reads the page.
remediation: Keep outbound credentials server-side, use scoped tokens instead of Basic auth, and never render the header.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the header form and the base64 payload length; it does not decode the pair.
scopeT: A body containing Basic authorization with a base64 value of at least sixteen characters.
fp: A page explaining how to format the header, without a credential value, is not reported.
recordDesc: An echoed Authorization header is a plaintext credential with a cosmetic encoding.
applicability: Debug endpoints, proxy panels and API playgrounds.
risk: The caller decodes the pair and reuses it against the upstream service.
why: Headers that carry credentials must never be echoed.
fix: Strip Authorization from every echoed request.
Exchange Basic auth for a short-lived token.
verifyT: Request the debug page and confirm no Basic value is present.

observation.body:
GET /api/v1/orders
Authorization: Basic cmFoaW06aHVudGVyMi1leGFtcGxl
Accept: application/json

Authentication

Send an Authorization header with the Basic scheme followed by the base64 pair.

title: OAuth client secret served in a response
description: The response carries a client_secret parameter with a value. A confidential client secret lets the holder impersonate the application at the identity provider.
remediation: Store client secrets in the server-side secret store and never place them in a page, query string or redirect target.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the parameter or field form and a value of twelve characters or more.
scopeT: A body containing a client_secret parameter or field with a value.
fp: A page that lists the parameter name without a value is not reported.
recordDesc: The client secret is the application password at the identity provider and can be used to request tokens for any user who consents.
applicability: OAuth callback pages, integration settings and token exchange logs.
risk: The caller can mint tokens as the application.
why: Confidential client credentials belong on the server only.
fix: Rotate the secret.
Keep it out of every response, log and redirect.
verifyT: Search the callback response and confirm no client_secret value is present.

observation.body:
OAuth setup

Provide client_id and client_secret to the token endpoint from your server.

title: SMTP credential served in a connection URI
description: The body carries an smtp:// URI with a user name and password. Mail credentials are often shared across applications and can be used to send mail as the organisation.
remediation: Move mail credentials to the secret store and reference them by name in configuration output.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the URI scheme and the userinfo segment.
scopeT: A body containing an smtp URI with a password in the userinfo segment.
fp: Documentation that shows the URI shape with placeholders is not reported, because a password of eight characters or more must follow the colon.
recordDesc: Mail credentials allow phishing from the organisation own domain, which bypasses most sender checks.
applicability: Configuration pages, health checks and diagnostic endpoints.
risk: The caller can send authenticated mail as the organisation.
why: Diagnostic output should name the host, never the credential.
fix: Mask credentials in connection strings.
Use app-specific mail credentials with send-only scope.
verifyT: Open the mail settings and confirm the password is masked.

observation.body:
Mail relay

Configure the relay as smtp://user:password@host:587 and keep it in the secret store.

title: Redis credential served in a connection URI
description: The body carries a redis:// URI with a password. A cache password usually protects the whole keyspace, including sessions and rate-limit counters.
remediation: Keep the cache URI server-side and return only the host and database index in diagnostics.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the redis or rediss scheme and the password segment.
scopeT: A body containing a redis URI with a password in the userinfo segment.
fp: A page that documents the URI shape with placeholders is not reported.
recordDesc: Cache credentials often reach every service in the estate and expose session and queue data.
applicability: Configuration dumps, health endpoints and deployment previews.
risk: The caller can read or flush the cache and hijack sessions stored there.
why: Connection strings are configuration, not output.
fix: Redact userinfo in every rendered connection string.
Use ACL-scoped cache users.
verifyT: Request the diagnostics page and confirm the URI has no password.

observation.body:
Cache

The cache is reached at redis://:password@host:6379 and the password lives in the vault.

title: MongoDB credential served in a connection URI
description: The body carries a mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// URI with a user name and password. Database credentials give direct access to the records the application serves.
remediation: Return the cluster host only, and keep credentials in the secret store.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the mongodb scheme and the userinfo segment.
scopeT: A body containing a MongoDB URI with a password in the userinfo segment.
fp: A documentation page with placeholders is not reported.
recordDesc: A database URI bypasses application authorisation entirely once it is known, because the driver connects with the privileges of the account it names.
applicability: Configuration pages, migration tooling and health checks.
risk: The caller connects directly to the database.
why: No screen needs the database password.
fix: Redact userinfo in diagnostic output.
Use per-service database users.
verifyT: Confirm the diagnostics page prints the host without credentials.

observation.body:
Database

Set the URI as mongodb://user:password@host/db in the environment file.

title: AMQP credential served in a connection URI
description: The body carries an amqp:// URI with a user name and password. Broker credentials allow publishing and consuming every queue the account can reach.
remediation: Keep broker credentials out of output and give each service its own vhost-scoped account.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the amqp or amqps scheme and the userinfo segment.
scopeT: A body containing an AMQP URI with a password in the userinfo segment.
fp: A page that shows the URI shape with placeholders is not reported.
recordDesc: A broker credential can read messages intended for other services and inject new ones.
applicability: Worker health pages, queue dashboards and deployment logs.
risk: The caller can consume or poison queued jobs.
why: Queue URIs are configuration, not page data.
fix: Mask credentials in rendered URIs.
Scope each service to its own vhost.
verifyT: Request the worker page and confirm the URI carries no password.

title: FTP credential served in a connection URI
description: The body carries an ftp:// URI with a user name and password. FTP credentials are frequently shared with partners and reused across batch jobs.
remediation: Move to SFTP with per-partner keys, and never render the URI with its userinfo.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the ftp or ftps scheme and the password segment.
scopeT: A body containing an FTP URI with a password in the userinfo segment.
fp: A page that documents the URI shape with placeholders is not reported.
recordDesc: FTP carries files in clear text and its credentials usually outlive the integration.
applicability: Batch integration status pages and partner configuration screens.
risk: The caller can read or overwrite exchanged files.
why: Integration pages should name the partner, not the credential.
fix: Migrate to key-based SFTP.
Redact userinfo in every rendered URI.
verifyT: Open the integration page and confirm no password is shown.

observation.body:
File exchange

Drop files at ftp://user:password@host/inbound; the password is provisioned by the partner.

title: JDBC connection properties carry a password in a response
description: The body carries a JDBC URL followed by a password property. JDBC properties are frequently logged in full because they travel as one string.
remediation: Keep the URL and its properties server-side and print only the host and schema.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the JDBC scheme and a password property in the same string.
scopeT: A body containing a jdbc URL and a password property.
fp: A page that documents the property names with placeholders is not reported.
recordDesc: A JDBC string with a password is a complete database login, and it is the form most likely to be copied into a ticket.
applicability: Connection-test endpoints and application server status pages.
risk: The caller connects to the database with application privileges.
why: Test endpoints should report success, not the credentials they used.
fix: Redact password properties before printing.
Use short-lived database tokens.
verifyT: Call the connection test and confirm the response has no password property.

title: LDAP bind credential served in a response
description: The body carries an LDAP URI with a bind DN and password. A service bind account usually reads the whole directory.
remediation: Use per-application bind accounts with minimal scope and keep the password out of output.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the ldap or ldaps scheme with a DN-shaped user and a password.
scopeT: A body containing an LDAP URI with a DN user and a password segment.
fp: A page with placeholders only is not reported.
recordDesc: A directory bind account exposes the employee directory and, with write rights, password resets.
applicability: Authentication status pages and directory integration settings.
risk: The caller can enumerate or modify directory entries.
why: Directory credentials must not be rendered.
fix: Mask the bind DN and password in every page.
Use a read-only scoped account.
verifyT: Open the directory settings and confirm the bind password is masked.

title: YAML password key served with a value
description: A served YAML document carries a password key with a value. YAML configuration is often pasted into tickets and runbooks, where the value outlives the service it belongs to.
remediation: Reference secrets by name and inject them at deploy time; never commit YAML with values.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the YAML key form and a value on the same line.
scopeT: A body containing a YAML password key with a plain or quoted value.
fp: A YAML reference where the value is a placeholder or a variable is not reported.
recordDesc: A YAML password is a plaintext credential in a file that is copied, diffed and archived.
applicability: Configuration pages, chart values and deployment manifests.
risk: The caller obtains credentials for a service the file configures.
why: Configuration files should point at secrets, not contain them.
fix: Replace the value with a secret reference.
Rotate the exposed password.
verifyT: Open the configuration file and confirm the password key carries a reference.

observation.body:
database:
  host: db.example
  password: dbpass-example
  user: app

Values

Set password: ${DB_PASSWORD} in your values file so the real value stays in the vault.

title: Java properties file serves a plaintext password
description: A served .properties document carries a datasource or spring password with a value. Properties files are the default Spring Boot configuration format and are frequently served from a misconfigured static path.
remediation: Use environment variables or a vault-backed property source, and never serve application.properties.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches a dotted password property with a value on the same line.
scopeT: A body containing a dotted password property and a plaintext value.
fp: A property that references an environment variable is not reported.
recordDesc: A properties file with a password is a complete credential for the datasource it configures.
applicability: Spring Boot applications with an exposed static or config path.
risk: The caller connects to the database or the external service.
why: Configuration should be injected, not served.
fix: Move the password to an environment variable.
Block static serving of configuration files.
verifyT: Request the properties path and confirm it is not served.

title: Django settings serve a database password
description: The body is a served Django settings module with a PASSWORD entry inside DATABASES. A settings module that is served instead of executed discloses every credential it configures.
remediation: Serve settings only through the framework and read secrets from the environment.
limitation: One response body. The rule needs the DATABASES block and a PASSWORD entry in the same body.
scopeT: A body containing DATABASES and a PASSWORD entry with a value.
fp: A settings documentation page that shows the key names without a value is not reported.
recordDesc: The settings module names the database, the cache, the mail relay and the secret key in one file.
applicability: Django deployments with a static alias that reaches the project directory.
risk: The caller obtains the database password and the surrounding configuration.
why: A settings module is source code, not a document.
fix: Keep settings outside every static root.
Read the password from the environment.
verifyT: Request the settings path and confirm it is not served.

observation.body:
Settings

The DATABASES dict reads PASSWORD from the environment in production.

title: ADO.NET connection string carries a password
description: The body carries a semicolon-delimited connection string with a Password key. Connection strings are logged whole by many stacks, so one page can seed a credential leak into the log pipeline.
remediation: Build the connection string at runtime from the secret store and never render it.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the key-value form with a semicolon delimiter.
scopeT: A body containing a connection string with Data Source or Initial Catalog and a Password key.
fp: A page with a placeholder password is not reported.
recordDesc: A rendered connection string gives the caller a direct database login with application privileges.
applicability: Health checks, admin diagnostics and legacy ASP.NET pages.
risk: The caller connects directly to the database.
why: Connection strings are the most commonly leaked credential in this shape.
fix: Redact Password and User ID before printing.
Use managed identities where available.
verifyT: Request the diagnostics page and confirm the string carries no Password key value.

observation.body:
Database

Use Server=host;Database=name;User Id=app;Password=***; in the local example.

title: JSON Web Token carried in a cookie
description: A Set-Cookie header carries a JSON Web Token as its value. The token is readable by page script unless the cookie is httpOnly, and its claims are visible to anyone who sees the header.
remediation: Store an opaque session id in an httpOnly cookie and keep the token on the server.
limitation: One response header. The rule recognises the three base64url segments and does not verify the signature.
scopeT: A Set-Cookie header whose value is a three-segment JSON Web Token.
fp: A cookie whose value is a random session id is not reported, because the three segment structure must be present.
recordDesc: A token in a readable cookie can be copied by any script on the page and replayed until it expires.
applicability: Single-page applications that keep the access token in a cookie.
risk: A cross-site scripting bug converts into full session takeover.
why: The browser can hold a session without exposing the token to script.
fix: Keep the token server-side and issue an opaque cookie.
Mark the cookie httpOnly and same-site.
verifyT: Inspect Set-Cookie and confirm the value is opaque.

title: .htpasswd credential file served from the web root
description: The body is an .htpasswd file: one username and one hash per line. The file protects a directory, so serving it hands over the account list and the hashes that guard it.
remediation: Deny access to dotfiles at the web server and move password files outside the document root.
limitation: One response body. The rule recognises the colon-separated user and hash lines; it does not crack the hashes.
scopeT: A body with at least two user:hash lines in htpasswd form.
fp: A documentation page that quotes one example line is not reported, because two credential lines must be present.
recordDesc: The account list plus hashes converts a protected directory into an offline cracking target.
applicability: Apache and nginx deployments that keep the password file inside the published directory.
risk: The caller learns the user names and can attack the hashes offline.
why: The password file is the lock, not a page.
fix: Return 403 for dotfile paths.
Store the file outside the document root.
verifyT: Request /.htpasswd and confirm a 403 or 404.

observation.body:
Basic auth

Create the file with htpasswd -c .htpasswd admin and keep it outside the document root.

title: .pgpass database credential file served
description: The body is a .pgpass file: host, port, database, user and password separated by colons. It is a complete set of PostgreSQL logins in one line per database.
remediation: Deny dotfile access and keep the pass file in the home directory of the service account only.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the five-field colon form; it does not test the credentials.
scopeT: A body with a five-field pgpass line ending in a password.
fp: A page that explains the file format with placeholder fields is not reported.
recordDesc: A served pgpass file gives the caller a working database login for every host, database and user it lists, without any further discovery step.
applicability: PostgreSQL clients configured through a published home directory.
risk: The caller connects to each listed database.
why: Credential files must never be reachable by URL.
fix: Block dotfiles at the web server.
Rotate the listed passwords.
verifyT: Request /.pgpass and confirm it is not served.

observation.body:
Password file

Each line holds host:port:database:user:password and the file must be chmod 600.

title: .netrc machine credentials served
description: The body is a .netrc file with a machine block and a login/password pair. Tools that read it authenticate non-interactively, so the file is a stored credential.
remediation: Remove the file from the document root and switch automation to scoped tokens.
limitation: One response body. The rule needs a machine block with both login and password.
scopeT: A body containing machine, login and password directives.
fp: A page with the directive names only is not reported.
recordDesc: A served netrc file authenticates CI jobs and deploy scripts without any further secret.
applicability: Deploy directories published by mistake.
risk: The caller can push to the repository or the artefact host as the automation account.
why: Automation credentials never belong in a served directory.
fix: Deny dotfiles.
Rotate the token and use a scoped one.
verifyT: Request /.netrc and confirm it is not served.

observation.body: machine git.example login deploy password tokenpass-example
machine registry.example login ci password registrypass-example

netrc

A machine block needs machine, login and password directives. Prefer tokens over passwords.

title: kubeconfig file served with its client key
description: The body is a kubeconfig with a cluster entry and client certificate data. It authenticates to the cluster as the identity embedded in the certificate.
remediation: Keep kubeconfig out of the web root, rotate the client certificate and use short-lived tokens.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the kubeconfig keys; it does not contact the cluster.
scopeT: A body containing clusters, users and client-certificate-data keys.
fp: A page that explains the kubeconfig layout without key material is not reported.
recordDesc: A served kubeconfig usually carries cluster-admin rights and every secret the cluster mounts.
applicability: Operator workstations or CI images that publish their home directory.
risk: The caller can read secrets, deploy workloads and pivot inside the cluster.
why: Cluster credentials are the highest-value file in most estates.
fix: Revoke the certificate.
Keep kubeconfig outside any served path.
verifyT: Request the file and confirm it is not served.

title: Terraform variable file served with values
description: The body is a .tfvars file with at least two assignments. Variable files hold the values the state depends on, often including account ids, endpoints and passwords.
remediation: Keep variable files out of the web root and load sensitive values from the environment or a vault.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the assignment form and does not judge the sensitivity of each value.
scopeT: A body with two or more name = "value" assignments in tfvars form.
fp: A page that shows one example assignment is not reported.
recordDesc: A variable file tells the caller which accounts, regions and endpoints the estate uses.
applicability: Infrastructure repositories published as static content.
risk: The caller maps the estate and finds any literal secret in the file.
why: Deployment values are configuration, not content.
fix: Block the path at the web server.
Move sensitive variables to the environment.
verifyT: Request the tfvars file and confirm a 403.

observation.body:
Variables

Assign values as region = "eu-west-1" in a tfvars file.

title: nginx configuration served from the web root
description: The body is an nginx configuration with server and location blocks. It reveals upstream hosts, internal paths, TLS settings and the include layout of the deployment.
remediation: Deny access to configuration paths and serve only compiled application content.
limitation: One response body. The rule matches the server and location block syntax; it does not parse the whole file.
scopeT: A body with nginx server and location blocks.
fp: A tutorial that quotes a configuration snippet in a code block is not reported, because the block must appear at the start of a line.
recordDesc: A configuration file maps the internal network and names the upstream services the caller can then probe.
applicability: Reverse proxies with a static route that reaches /etc or a checkout.
risk: The caller learns internal hostnames and the routing topology.
why: Server configuration is never page content.
fix: Return 403 for configuration paths.
Keep configuration outside the document root.
verifyT: Request the configuration path and confirm a 403.

nginx

Define a server block and add a location for each upstream you proxy.

title: php.ini configuration served from the web root
description: The body is a php.ini with at least two directives. The file names the extensions, the upload limits and often the session storage path of the deployment.
remediation: Keep php.ini outside the document root and deny access to .ini paths.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads two or more directive assignments in ini form.

observation.body: Our policy is default-src self delivered as a header, not in a meta tag.

title: Meta tag sends CSP reports over plaintext HTTP
description: A meta policy sets report-uri to an http endpoint. Every violation report, which includes the blocked URL and the page address, then travels in clear text.
remediation: Point report-uri at an https collector and prefer the Reporting API with Report-To.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the report-uri value in the meta policy.
scopeT: A response body with a meta CSP and an http report-uri.
fp: A page that shows the directive without an http URL is not reported.
recordDesc: Violation reports describe the pages the user visits, and plaintext transport exposes that trail to the network.
applicability: Applications that configure reporting in the template.
risk: A network observer learns which pages triggered which violations.
why: Reporting endpoints are part of the security configuration.
fix: Change report-uri to https.
Move the policy to a header.
verifyT: Inspect the policy and confirm the collector is https.

observation.body: Set report-uri to the https collector, for example report-uri https://reports.example/csp.

title: JSONP callback endpoint served
description: The response is a JSONP wrapper: a caller-supplied callback name around a data object. Any origin can load the endpoint as a script and read the data through the callback.
remediation: Remove JSONP support and serve CORS-restricted JSON instead.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the callback wrapper; it does not vary the callback name.
scopeT: A body with a function-call wrapper around a JSON object.
fp: A page that documents a callback parameter without a wrapped payload is not reported.
recordDesc: JSONP bypasses the same-origin policy by design, so the data is readable by any site that knows the endpoint.
applicability: Legacy AJAX endpoints and cross-domain widgets.
risk: A third-party page reads the response on behalf of a logged-in user.
why: JSONP cannot be authorised per origin.
fix: Serve JSON with an explicit CORS allowlist.
Require a token for the endpoint.
verifyT: Request the endpoint with a different callback and confirm JSON is returned instead.

observation.body: The legacy endpoint accepted a callback parameter and wrapped the JSON in a function call.

title: Server-side include directive served unprocessed
description: The body contains raw SSI directives such as include or exec. The server did not evaluate them, which usually means the file was read from disk and returned as text.
remediation: Enable SSI only where it is intended and never serve template sources.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the directive comments and does not attempt to execute them.
scopeT: A body containing an SSI include or exec directive.
fp: A page that shows an SSI example in a code block with escaped angle brackets is not reported.
recordDesc: Unprocessed directives show that the response is a source file rather than a rendered page.
applicability: Misconfigured static hosting over a template directory.
risk: The caller learns the template layout and can request the included files directly.
why: Served template source is a directory listing in disguise.
fix: Render the page through the application server.
Deny direct access to template directories.
verifyT: Request the page and confirm no SSI comment markers appear.

observation.body: SSI uses <!--#include --> comments, which the server evaluates before sending.

title: JSP source served instead of a rendered page
description: The body is a JSP source file with its page directive and scriptlets. The container returned the source, so the caller can read the queries, credentials and business logic in it.
remediation: Serve JSP only through the container and deny direct access to source paths.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the page directive and a scriptlet block.
scopeT: A body with a JSP page directive and a scriptlet.
fp: A documentation page with escaped source is not reported, because the page directive must be unescaped.
recordDesc: JSP source contains the SQL statements and the credentials the page uses, in the form the server executes.
applicability: Application servers misrouted to serve the webapp directory as static files.
risk: The caller reads database queries, internal hosts and any hard-coded secrets.
why: Source behind a renderer is never content.
fix: Route the path to the container.
Deny .jsp sources as static files.
verifyT: Request the file and confirm it renders rather than prints.

<% String q = "SELECT * FROM users"; %>

title: PHP source served instead of an executed page
description: The body is PHP source with an opening tag and statements. When the handler is missing or misconfigured, the server returns the code that the interpreter should have executed.
remediation: Restore the PHP handler for the path and deny serving .php files as static content.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the opening tag and a statement terminator; it does not parse the code.
scopeT: A body with a PHP opening tag and at least one statement.
fp: A page that shows escaped PHP in a code block is not reported.
recordDesc: PHP source names the database credentials, the include paths and the logic the caller is attacking.
applicability: Server configuration changes that removed the PHP handler.
risk: The caller reads credentials and application logic directly.
why: Source is not a response body.
fix: Re-enable the PHP handler for the path.
Block source files at the web server.
verifyT: Request the page and confirm it renders.

observation.body: Escape the tag as <?php when you show a snippet in documentation.

title: HTML comment carries a credential
description: A comment in the served markup names a password, token or key and gives its value. Comments survive templating and are delivered to every visitor.
remediation: Strip development comments from deployed templates and rotate anything that appeared in one.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads comment text with a credential marker and a value.
scopeT: A body with an HTML comment naming a credential and a value.
fp: A page that discusses comments without a value after the marker is not reported.
recordDesc: Comment credentials are the classic forgotten secret: they are invisible on the page but present in every response and cache.
applicability: Templates with developer notes left in place.
risk: The caller reads a working credential from the page source.
why: The source of every page is public.
fix: Remove the comment and rotate the credential.
Fail the build on marker words inside comments.
verifyT: View the page source and confirm no credential appears in a comment.

observation.body: Never leave a password in a comment.

title: Redirect carries a token in the URL fragment
description: The Location header points at a fragment that names a token. Fragments are not sent to the server, but they stay in browser history and are readable by any script on the destination page.
remediation: Deliver the token in a short-lived code and exchange it server-side.
limitation: One response header. The rule reads the fragment of the redirect target.
scopeT: A Location header whose fragment contains an access token parameter.
fp: A redirect to a documentation anchor is not reported, because the fragment must carry a token parameter.
recordDesc: Token fragments are the OAuth implicit flow residue: they persist in history and in any extension or script on the page.
applicability: Single-page login callbacks that still use the implicit flow.
risk: A script on the destination page or a shared machine history exposes the token.
why: Tokens in URLs outlive the request.
fix: Switch to the authorisation code flow with PKCE.
Keep tokens out of the URL entirely.
verifyT: Trace the login redirect and confirm the fragment carries no token.

title: Redirect carries a bare token in the query string
description: The Location header points at a query string with a token parameter. Query strings are written to access logs, proxy logs and Referer headers, so a bare token escapes the flow it was minted for.
remediation: Send a single-use code instead, bound to the client and to a short lifetime.
limitation: One response header. The rule reads the query string of the redirect target and requires a token-shaped value.
scopeT: A Location header with a token parameter and a value of sixteen characters or more.
fp: A redirect that carries the word token without a value is not reported.
recordDesc: A token in a redirect URL is copied into access logs, proxy logs and Referer headers before the browser ever uses it, which outlives the flow it was minted for.
applicability: Password-reset links, invitation links and magic-link logins.
risk: Anyone with log access replays the token.
why: URLs are the least private place a credential can travel.
fix: Use a short-lived single-use code.
Redact token parameters in access logs.
verifyT: Trigger the flow and confirm the token is not in the Location header.

title: Cookie attribute value contains a semicolon
description: A Set-Cookie attribute value is quoted and contains a semicolon. Browsers end the attribute at the separator, so the rest of the value is parsed as new attributes or dropped.
remediation: Never put a semicolon inside a cookie attribute; encode the value or use a different attribute.
limitation: One response header. The rule reads the quoted attribute value.
scopeT: A Set-Cookie header with a quoted attribute containing a semicolon.
fp: A cookie whose value is quoted without a semicolon is not reported.
recordDesc: Silent truncation of an attribute changes the security properties the author intended, often turning a scoped cookie into a broad one.
applicability: Frameworks that build the Path or Domain attribute from user configuration.
risk: The cookie is stored with different attributes than the code intended.
why: Attribute parsing is stricter than most string builders assume.
fix: Validate attribute values against the cookie grammar.
Encode or drop the offending characters.
verifyT: Inspect the Set-Cookie header and confirm no attribute value carries a semicolon.

title: Cookie carries an expired date and a positive Max-Age
description: A Set-Cookie header sets an Expires date in the past and a positive Max-Age at the same time. Browsers prefer Max-Age, so the cookie that looks expired is actually persistent.
remediation: Emit one lifetime attribute; delete a cookie with Max-Age=0 and an Expires in the past together.
limitation: One response header. The rule reads both lifetime attributes in the same header.
scopeT: A Set-Cookie header with a past Expires year and a positive Max-Age.
fp: A cookie with only one lifetime attribute is not reported.
recordDesc: The contradiction is invisible in review and changes retention silently, which matters for logout and consent.
applicability: Hand-written cookie builders and framework migrations.
risk: A cookie the code believes is deleted continues to be stored and sent.
why: Lifetime attributes must agree.
fix: Emit a single lifetime attribute.
Test the logout path for a removed cookie.
verifyT: Inspect Set-Cookie on logout and confirm Max-Age=0 with a past Expires.

title: Inline script assigns document.domain
description: An inline script assigns document.domain. The assignment relaxes the same-origin policy for the page and any frame it talks to, and browsers are deprecating it because of that.
remediation: Remove the assignment and use postMessage with an origin check or a shared subdomain.
limitation: One response body. The rule reads the assignment inside a script element.
scopeT: A response body with a document.domain assignment.
fp: A page that discusses the API without an assignment is not reported.
recordDesc: Relaxing the origin boundary lets a compromised sibling subdomain read the page and its frames.
applicability: Legacy single-sign-on integrations that span subdomains.
risk: Any script on a sibling subdomain can read this page origin.
why: Origin relaxation is global to the page and its frames.
fix: Use postMessage with an explicit target origin.
Move both apps under one origin.
verifyT: Search the page scripts for a document.domain assignment.

observation.body: Do not assign document.domain; use postMessage with an origin check.

scopeT: A response body with the Temporal title and a Workflows marker.

risk: The caller reads every workflow payload and can signal running executions.
why: The payload store is production data.

Encrypt payloads and restrict the codec key.

Restrict the portal to the corporate network.

Alert on policy changes.
